handNote.p: The [h] character in Scribe 1 is distinguished by a sharp angle at the top of the first vertical as the quill changes direction, a bowed crossbar, a round loop, and a very slight foot at the base of the second vertical. The word-end [m] and [n] glyphs conclude with a backward flourish that stretches as far as the penultimate minim.

More cramped than Scribe 1, with a slightly slanted character. This scribe uses a horizontal, straight crossbar, an oval loop, and an upwardly angled final tick. The final backstroke of [m] and [n] is short, barely passing the final minim.
The [h] written by Scribe 3 is similar to that of Scribe 1, although slightly more compact. The final stroke of [m] and [n] curves back on itself, nearly touching the top of the final minim.
The [h] written by Scribe 4 has a perpendicular crossbar, an oversize loop, and a prominent final foot. The final stroke of [m] and [n] is tall, with only a slight curvature.

The [h] is tall and narrow, with a bowed cross-stroke that begins at the top of the vertical, and a minuscule tick at the foot of the second vertical. The [m] has a long, low finial that finishes above the penultimate minim

origin.p: The origins of this manuscript are unknown, but it has been carbon dated to have been made sometime between 1404 and 1438.

provenance.p: Any history between 1404 and 1576 is missing and unknown.

Owned by Rudolph II of Habsburg during his reign in Prague from 1576 to 1611. In 1599, Karl Widemann sold Rudolph II several books, one of which was likely the Voynich Manuscript, but this is not confirmed.

Jacobus Horcicky de Tepenecz owned the manuscript in 1622. This is noted in an inscription on folio 1r which reads Jacobi de Tepenecz under uv light. The manuscript was likely owned by someone else and given to him as a part of his inheritance.
Owned by Georgius Barschius potentially sometime between 1627 and 1637.
Johannes Marcus Marci of Kronland was gifted Barschius' alchemical library in 1677, which included the Voynich Manuscript.
Wilfred M. Voynich acquired the manuscript in 1912 at the Villa Mondragone in Italy
H. P. Kraus purchases the manuscript from Ethel Voynich, Wilfrid Voynich's widow.
Given to the Beinecke Library by H. P. Kraus

msContents.summary: The latest release of the Zandbergen-Landini transliteration of 1999 in the IVTFF 2.0 format. It is a complete transliteration, including all 5389 loci that have been identified in the MS. It uses the Eva alphabet, including the high-ascii extensions. The file has been corrected in numerous places. Some parts of the text inside folds of the pages still need to be added.
